title: What "the model travels to the data" means for AI training and your privacy
excerpt: Some new frameworks let AI learn from sensitive records without the records ever being handed over. Here is how that works, what protects you, and what to ask.

sources.title: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, India: Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training, draft for discussion
NIST: NIST finalizes guidelines for evaluating differential privacy guarantees (SP 800-226)
ANI: MeitY launches DEPA handbook to enable secure data sharing for AI training

body_html:
Useful AI often needs to learn from sensitive information: hospital records, bank transactions, public-service files. The usual worry is simple. Once that data is copied to whoever is building the AI, the people it describes lose control of it. A growing idea in AI policy turns this around: instead of sending the data to the model, the model is sent to the data.

Where the phrase comes from

The idea is at the centre of a draft framework from India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training, launched at an event in Bengaluru on 31 October 2026. It is a draft for discussion, not a law. But the techniques it describes are used in many countries, so the questions it raises apply everywhere.

How it works

In the DEPA draft, the institution that holds the data, such as a hospital or bank, prepares and de-identifies it. The data then stays inside a registered "secure data environment": protected hardware where computing happens, but where outsiders cannot simply copy what is inside. A developer who wants to train a model sends the model in, trains it on approved data, and takes out only the trained model, not the raw records.

The draft also mentions other ways to learn from data without pooling it in one place. Federated learning trains a model in several locations and combines only what the model learned. Secure multi-party computation lets several parties compute a result together without revealing their own inputs.

The protections around it

Keeping the data in place is only one layer. The draft lists others:

  • De-identification. Personal data is stripped of direct identifiers before use, and raw personal data is not to be shared.
  • Differential privacy. Calibrated random noise is added so that no single person can be picked out, with limits that are set, monitored and audited.
  • Purpose limits. Electronic contracts state what the data may be used for and enforce those terms.
  • Audit trails. Tamper-resistant logs record who did what.
  • Checks before release. Trained models must pass independent validation, including bias and fairness audits and security testing, before pilot use.

What it does not solve on its own

These methods reduce risk; they do not remove it. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in its guidelines on evaluating differential privacy, warns that noise applied the wrong way can weaken privacy or make data less useful, and that small groups may need extra protection because they stand out. In NIST's words: "There is no simple answer for how to balance privacy with usefulness."

That is why the DEPA draft also requires checks on the finished model, not only on the training setup. And consent still counts: the draft says data-sharing procedures should cover consent, and people should know when their records are used to train AI and for what purpose.

Questions you can ask

  • Was my data used to train this AI, and was it de-identified first?
  • Did the raw data leave the organisation that holds it?
  • What is it allowed to be used for, and who checks that?
  • Was the finished model tested independently before release?
  • Who do I contact if I think my information was misused?

Why it matters for people staying in charge

Humasure's Directive 5, Private by default, asks that AI products protect personal information without people having to fight for it. Directive 6, Secure and supported, covers the security of the environments where data and models live, and Directive 9, Accountable, asks that someone answers for how data is used. Approaches that let AI learn without taking people's records are a promising step, as long as they are checked. You can find more questions on our Questions to ask page.
